overview.title: Computation graphs of the model and of a toy example; the forward pass
overview.chapter: 2 The mathematical building blocks of neural networks
overview.section: 2.4 The engine of neural networks: Gradient-based optimization
overview.main_topic: Drawing the two-layer model and a one-layer scalar toy model as computation graphs, running the forward pass with concrete numbers, and preparing to reverse the graph for the backward pass
overview.central_idea: A model is a graph of operations fed by input nodes (data and parameters). Running the forward pass means propagating concrete values from the input nodes down to loss_val; with x = 2, w = 3, b = 1 and y_true = 4 the toy graph gives x1 = 6, x2 = 7, loss_val = 3. The backward pass will reverse every edge and ask how much each node's output varies with its input.
overview.importance: These three figures are the visual backbone of the backpropagation explanation. Figure 2.21 shows that the real model is just a bigger version of the toy graph; figures 2.22 and 2.23 fix the concrete numbers that p.73 and p.74 differentiate.
learning_objectives: Read figure 2.21 and map each node to a term of the nested expression on p.70.
Identify input nodes (x, y_true, w, b) versus operation nodes (*, +, loss) in figure 2.22.
Carry out the forward pass of figure 2.23 by hand: x1 = 6, x2 = 7, loss_val = 3.
Explain what 'reversing the graph' means and what question each reversed edge answers (grad(B, A)).
prerequisites: The nested model expression loss(y_true, softmax(matmul(relu(matmul(inputs, W1) + b1), W2) + b2)) (p.70)
Computation graphs as directed acyclic graphs of tensor operations (p.71)
The toy setup: scalars w, b, x and the loss abs(y_true - y) (p.71)

summary:
This page is almost entirely figures. **Figure 2.21** draws the first MNIST model as a computation graph: the input `x` flows down through `dot` (with `W1`), `+` (with `b1`), `relu`, `dot` (with `W2`), `+` (with `b2`), `softmax`, and finally `loss` (with `y_true`), producing `loss_val`. Parameters (`W1`, `b1`, `W2`, `b2`) are drawn as green input circles on the left, data (`x`, `y_true`) as blue circles, and operations as grey boxes. This is the expression of p.70 drawn as a directed acyclic graph.

**Figure 2.22** is the simplified scalar graph announced on p.71: `x` and `w` feed a `*` node producing `x1`; `x1` and `b` feed a `+` node producing `x2`; `x2` and `y_true` feed `loss`, producing `loss_val`. The text then sets concrete values for the four input nodes (**figure 2.23**): `x = 2`, `w = 3`, `b = 1`, `y_true = 4`. Propagating these values through the graph from top to bottom gives `x1 = 6`, `x2 = 7` and `loss_val = 3`. This is the **forward pass**.

The last paragraph begins the next step: "reverse" the graph. For every edge from `A` to `B`, create an opposite edge from `B` to `A` and ask "How much does `B` vary when `A` varies?", that is, what is `grad(B, A)`. The sentence continues on p.73, where each reversed edge is annotated with its gradient (figure 2.24) and the chain rule is applied along paths to obtain `grad(loss_val, w) = 2` and `grad(loss_val, b) = 1`.

paragraphs.excerpt: Let's set concrete values for the "input nodes" in the graph
paragraphs.what_it_says: (Merged with the fragments p072_e18 and p072_e20.) Set concrete values for the input nodes of the toy graph: the input x, the target y_true, and the parameters w and b (figure 2.23). Propagate these values to all nodes, from top to bottom, until loss_val is reached. This is the forward pass.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Figure 2.23 shows the values: x = 2, w = 3, b = 1, y_true = 4. The multiplication node outputs x1 = 2 * 3 = 6, the addition node outputs x2 = 6 + 1 = 7, and the loss node outputs loss_val = abs(4 - 7) = 3. 'Input nodes' are the nodes with no incoming edges; they include both data (x, y_true) and parameters (w, b), because for the purpose of evaluating the graph both are just given numbers.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: The forward pass is step 2 and 3 of the training loop on p.68 (run the model, compute the loss). It also fixes the intermediate values (x1 = 6, x2 = 7) at which the local derivatives of the backward pass will be evaluated; without them the chain-rule factors on p.73 could not be computed.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Evaluating a DAG in topological order: each operation node is computed once all of its inputs are available, so values flow strictly from inputs to the single output loss_val.

terminology.meaning: Nodes of the graph with no incoming edges whose values are given: here x, y_true, w and b.
Propagating input values through every operation of the graph until the loss value is produced.

connections: p.68: Steps 2-3 of mini-batch SGD (forward pass, compute loss).
p.71: The toy graph and the loss abs(y_true - y) were defined there.
p.73: The backward pass uses these forward values (x2 = 7 versus y_true = 4; x = 2) to compute the edge gradients.

paragraphs.excerpt: Now let's "reverse" the graph: for each edge in the graph going
paragraphs.what_it_says: (Merged with the fragment p072_e24; the sentence ends on p.73.) Reverse the graph: for each edge going from A to B, create an opposite edge from B to A and ask how much B varies when A varies, i.e. what is grad(B, A).
paragraphs.what_it_means: The forward graph answers 'what is B given A?'; the reversed graph answers 'how sensitive is B to A?'. Each reversed edge carries one local derivative: grad(x1, w), grad(x1, x), grad(x2, x1), grad(x2, b), grad(loss_val, x2). These are the per-link factors that the chain rule (p.71) multiplies along a path.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This reversal is the construction of the backward pass. Once every edge has its local derivative, the gradient of loss_val with respect to any node is obtained by multiplying along the path from loss_val back to that node (and summing if several paths exist, p.74).
paragraphs.technical_idea: Reverse-mode differentiation: the backward graph has the same nodes and reversed edges, each labelled with a local derivative evaluated at the forward values.

terminology.meaning: How much node B varies per unit variation of node A: the derivative of B with respect to A, the label of the reversed edge from B to A.
The graph with all edges reversed and annotated with local derivatives (figure 2.24, p.73).

connections: p.73: Figure 2.24 shows the reversed, annotated graph and lists each grad value with its justification.
p.74: Figure 2.25 highlights the path from loss_val to w; the NOTE explains summing over multiple paths.

concepts.name: Computation graph
concepts.definition: A directed acyclic graph whose nodes are operations and input values and whose edges carry the values from producer to consumer.
concepts.intuition: Figure 2.21: data and parameters enter as circles at the top and left; grey operation boxes transform them step by step down to loss_val.
concepts.technical: Figure 2.21 has operation nodes dot, +, relu, dot, +, softmax, loss and input nodes x, W1, b1, W2, b2, y_true. Figure 2.22 is the one-layer scalar version with nodes *, +, loss and inputs x, w, b, y_true.
concepts.significance: The structure on which the forward pass (values flow down) and the backward pass (gradients flow up) are both defined.
concepts.example: In figure 2.21, the node sequence dot -> + -> relu is exactly the first Dense layer relu(dot(input, W1) + b1).
concepts.misconception: Parameters are not 'inside' the operation nodes; they are separate input nodes feeding the dot and + operations, which is why gradients with respect to them can be read off the reversed edges.

concepts.name: Forward pass
concepts.definition: Propagating concrete values from the input nodes of a computation graph through every operation until the loss value is obtained.
concepts.intuition: Fill in the numbers top to bottom: 2 * 3 = 6, 6 + 1 = 7, |4 - 7| = 3.
concepts.technical: Figure 2.23: x = 2, w = 3 -> x1 = 6; x1 = 6, b = 1 -> x2 = 7; x2 = 7, y_true = 4 -> loss_val = 3. Evaluation follows a topological order of the DAG.
concepts.significance: Produces both the loss (the quantity to minimize) and the intermediate values at which the backward pass evaluates every local derivative.
concepts.example: For the full model, the forward pass is the computation of loss(y_true, softmax(matmul(relu(matmul(inputs, W1) + b1), W2) + b2)) on a batch.
concepts.misconception: The forward pass alone does not tell you how to change w and b; it only gives the current loss. Direction and magnitude of change come from the backward pass.

concepts.name: Backward pass (reversed graph)
concepts.definition: The graph with every edge A -> B reversed into B -> A and annotated with grad(B, A), how much B varies when A varies.
concepts.intuition: Turn every arrow around and label it with a sensitivity.
concepts.technical: The labels are local derivatives evaluated at the forward values; the chain rule then multiplies them along paths from loss_val to any parameter (p.73).
concepts.significance: Step 4 of the training loop (p.68): computing the gradient of the loss with respect to the parameters.
concepts.example: The edge w -> * becomes * -> w with label grad(x1, w) = x = 2 (p.73).
concepts.misconception: Reversing the graph does not recompute the forward values; it adds derivative labels to the existing structure.

math.title: Forward pass of the toy graph with the values of figure 2.23
math.latex: \begin{aligned} x_1 &= x \cdot w = 2 \cdot 3 = 6 \\ x_2 &= x_1 + b = 6 + 1 = 7 \\ \text{loss\_val} &= \lvert y_{\text{true}} - x_2 \rvert = \lvert 4 - 7 \rvert = 3 \end{aligned}
math.source_text: x1 = 6, x2 = 7, loss_val = 3 (labels in figure 2.23, with input nodes x = 2, w = 3, b = 1, y_true = 4)

variables.meaning: Output of the + node; this is the model's prediction y.
Absolute error between target and prediction.

math.operations: A multiplication, an addition and an absolute difference, applied in graph order.
math.purpose: To obtain the loss for the current parameters and to record the intermediate values needed by the backward pass.
math.interpretation: The prediction 7 overshoots the target 4 by 3. Since x2 > y_true, decreasing x2 (and hence w or b) would reduce the loss; the backward pass on p.73 quantifies this.
math.intuition: Plug numbers into the pipeline and read off the result at the bottom.
math.numerical_example: Changing w from 3 to 2.9 gives x1 = 5.8, x2 = 6.8, loss_val = 2.8: a decrease of 0.2 for a change of -0.1 in w, consistent with grad(loss_val, w) = 2 found on p.73.

deeper.title: Reading figure 2.21 against the nested expression
deeper.body:
Figure 2.21 and the one-line expression on p.70 contain the same information. Walking down the figure:

| Figure node | Inputs | Expression fragment | Output shape (MNIST) |
|---|---|---|---|
| dot | x, W1 | matmul(inputs, W1) | (batch, 512) |
| + | previous, b1 | ... + b1 | (batch, 512) |
| relu | previous | relu(...) | (batch, 512) |
| dot | previous, W2 | matmul(..., W2) | (batch, 10) |
| + | previous, b2 | ... + b2 | (batch, 10) |
| softmax | previous | softmax(...) | (batch, 10) |
| loss | previous, y_true | loss(y_true, ...) | scalar |

The colour coding in the figure is worth noticing: green circles are trainable parameters (the nodes whose gradients we want), blue circles are data (fixed for a given batch), grey boxes are operations. The toy graph of figure 2.22 keeps one node of each kind of operation (one dot, one +, one loss) and drops relu, the second layer and softmax. Shapes are not stated on the page; they follow from the model definition on p.42 (Dense(512), Dense(10)).

deeper.title: The forward pass as a worksheet
deeper.body:
Figure 2.23 is best reproduced by hand before reading p.73:

1. Write the four input values next to their nodes: x = 2, w = 3, b = 1, y_true = 4.
2. The * node has both inputs available: x1 = 2 * 3 = 6.
3. The + node now has both inputs: x2 = 6 + 1 = 7.
4. The loss node has x2 = 7 and y_true = 4: loss_val = |4 - 7| = 3.

Keep x1 = 6, x2 = 7 and the fact that x2 > y_true in view. On p.73 the local derivatives are: grad(loss_val, x2) = 1 (the loss is |4 - x2| and x2 is on the side where increasing x2 increases the loss), grad(x2, x1) = 1 and grad(x2, b) = 1 (addition), grad(x1, w) = x = 2 (multiplication). All of them use the forward values.

deeper.title: Why reverse the edges instead of differentiating forward?
deeper.body: Beyond the book: one could also propagate derivatives in the forward direction, carrying 'how much does this node change when w changes' alongside each value (this is called forward-mode differentiation). But that requires one forward sweep per parameter: one for w, one for b, and for the MNIST model 407,050 sweeps. Reversing the graph (reverse-mode differentiation, which is what backpropagation is) instead carries 'how much does loss_val change when this node changes' from the single output back to all inputs in one sweep. Because a network has one scalar loss and very many parameters, the reverse direction is overwhelmingly cheaper, which is why figure 2.24 reverses the arrows.

visualizations.title: Figure 2.23: forward pass with concrete values
visualizations.why: Shows the toy graph of figure 2.22 with the input values of figure 2.23 (x = 2, w = 3, b = 1, y_true = 4) and the values computed at each node: x1 = 6, x2 = 7, loss_val = 3.

visualizations.title: Step through the forward pass, then reverse the graph
visualizations.why: The widget uses the same one-layer graph as figures 2.22-2.23 (x, w, b combined into a prediction, then a loss) with the page's values x = 2, w = 3, b = 1, y_true = 4; its forward values x * w = 6 and 6 + 1 = 7 match figure 2.23. Its loss is the squared error rather than the book's absolute error, so the loss value and the final gradient factor differ from the book's 3 and 1, but the reversal of edges it animates is exactly what the last paragraph of the page describes.

misconceptions.claim: Only the data x and y_true are input nodes; the parameters live inside the operations.
misconceptions.correction: In figures 2.21-2.23 the parameters w, b (and W1, b1, W2, b2) are drawn as input nodes alongside x and y_true. Operations have no internal state; this is what lets the backward pass assign a gradient to each parameter edge.

misconceptions.claim: The forward pass already tells you which way to move w and b.
misconceptions.correction: The forward pass only yields loss_val = 3. The direction and magnitude of the update come from the gradients computed in the backward pass (p.73).

misconceptions.claim: Reversing the graph means running the operations backward to recover the inputs.
misconceptions.correction: Reversing creates edges B -> A labelled with grad(B, A), the sensitivity of B to A. It is a derivative bookkeeping device, not an inversion of the computation.

takeaways: Figure 2.21 draws the two-layer model as a computation graph: dot, +, relu, dot, +, softmax, loss, with the parameters W1, b1, W2, b2 and data x, y_true as input nodes.
Figure 2.22 is the one-layer scalar toy graph: x and w -> *, then + b, then loss against y_true.
The forward pass propagates input values top to bottom: with x = 2, w = 3, b = 1, y_true = 4 we get x1 = 6, x2 = 7, loss_val = 3.
Reversing the graph creates an edge B -> A for every edge A -> B, labelled with grad(B, A): how much B varies when A varies. This is the backward pass, continued on p.73.

questions.question: Using the input values of figure 2.23 (x = 2, w = 3, b = 1, y_true = 4), compute x1, x2 and loss_val.
questions.explanation: Propagate the values through the * node, the + node and the loss node abs(y_true - y) in that order; the figure labels x1 = 6, x2 = 7 and loss_val = 3 confirm it.

questions.question: Which nodes are the 'input nodes' of the toy computation graph in figure 2.23?
questions.explanation: The page says: 'set concrete values for the input nodes in the graph, that is, the input x, the target y_true, w and b'. Parameters count as input nodes; x1, x2 and loss_val are computed by operations.

questions.question: In figure 2.21, which three consecutive operation nodes implement the first Dense layer, and which input nodes feed them?
questions.answer: dot (fed by x and W1), + (fed by b1), and relu; together they compute relu(dot(x, W1) + b1).
questions.explanation: Figure 2.21 draws the chain dot -> + -> relu at the top, with W1 entering dot and b1 entering +, matching the first layer in the expression on p.70 and the layer formula on p.63.

questions.question: What does it mean to 'reverse' the computation graph, and what question is attached to each reversed edge?
questions.answer: For every edge A -> B, add an opposite edge B -> A and ask how much B varies when A varies, i.e. compute grad(B, A). The reversed, annotated graph is the backward pass.
questions.explanation: The page's last paragraph describes exactly this construction; p.73 carries it out and annotates each reversed edge (figure 2.24).

questions.question: Which operations of the full model (figure 2.21) are omitted in the simplified toy graph (figure 2.22)?
options: relu, the second dot and +, and softmax
Nothing is omitted; only the values are scalar
questions.answer: relu, the second dot and +, and softmax
questions.explanation: Figure 2.22 keeps one multiplication (the scalar version of dot), one addition and the loss; the relu, the entire second layer (dot, +) and softmax are dropped, as the text on p.71 said ('only one linear layer').

questions.question: Before turning to p.73, predict the values of grad(x1, w), grad(x2, x1), grad(x2, b) and grad(loss_val, x2) for the forward values of figure 2.23, and say which forward values each depends on.
questions.answer: grad(x1, w) = x = 2 (depends on x); grad(x2, x1) = 1 and grad(x2, b) = 1 (addition, independent of values); grad(loss_val, x2) = 1 because x2 = 7 > y_true = 4 so the loss |4 - x2| grows with x2 (depends on which side of y_true the prediction lies).
questions.explanation: These are exactly the four values annotated in figure 2.24 on p.73. Only grad(x1, w) and grad(loss_val, x2) depend on the forward pass, which is why the forward pass must be run first.
